core: The Demographic Transition Model (DTM) as a stage-based generalization of how birth and death rates change with development
Stage 1: high birth rates and high death rates producing a low, stable population
Stage 2: death rates fall (better food, medicine, sanitation) while birth rates stay high, producing rapid growth
Stage 3: birth rates fall (urbanization, education, family planning, lower child mortality) so growth slows
Stage 4: low birth and low death rates producing a stable, high population
Stage 5 (debated): birth rates below death rates producing population decline
The DTM as a model/generalization grounded in the historical experience of industrialized (largely European) countries, with stated usefulness and limitations
supporting: The 'growth gap' mechanism: death rates fall before birth rates, opening a temporary gap that drives rapid growth
Replacement-level fertility (~2.1 births per woman) as the threshold near which a population stabilizes without migration
Dated global figures (UN WPP 2024) to ground the model in current conditions
outOfScope: Formal definitions of birth rate, death rate, and total fertility rate (owned by the population topic; referenced only)
Detailed treatment of migration's push-pull drivers (owned by the migration topic; noted only as a DTM limitation)
Measures and indices of economic development and human development (owned by their own topics)

claims.claim: The Demographic Transition Model describes how a society shifts from high birth and high death rates to low birth and low death rates as it develops from a pre-industrial to an industrialized economy.
In Stage 1, both birth rates and death rates are high, so the population stays low and roughly stable; this describes most of human history.
In Stage 2, death rates fall sharply because of improvements in food supply, medicine, and sanitation, while birth rates remain high, producing rapid population growth.
In Stage 3, birth rates begin to fall as child survival improves, families become smaller, women's roles change, and access to family planning rises, so population growth decelerates.
In Stage 4, both birth and death rates are low, so the population is large but roughly stable, with growth near zero.

A debated Stage 5 describes fertility falling below the death rate at very high development, leading to population decline; this stage is uncertain because only a few societies have reached this level.

The DTM is a generalization built on the historical experience of industrializing European countries; it can be applied elsewhere, but not every country or region fits the model exactly, and the timing and drivers vary.
The classic DTM tracks only births and deaths within a closed population and does not incorporate migration, which is a recognized limitation when applying it to real countries.
The world population reached about 8.2 billion in 2024 and is projected by the UN to peak at around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s before declining to roughly 10.2 billion by 2100.
Replacement-level fertility is about 2.1 births per woman; as of the UN's 2024 assessment, in more than half of all countries and areas fertility is already below that level.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many stages the model has
positions: Many textbooks present a four-stage model (Stages 1-4).
Others add a fifth stage in which sub-replacement fertility drives decline.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a four-stage classic model plus a debated Stage 5, matching how Our World in Data and current data (widespread sub-replacement fertility) frame it, while flagging Stage 5 as uncertain.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept students use to organize information') with no substantive claims about stages, drivers, or data; none of it was usable as evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate definition with the actual model: a stage-based account of birth and death rate change.
Added the four classic stages and the debated Stage 5 with their drivers.
Added the model-vs-reality framing (European origin, imperfect fit, no migration) required by the subject source-map.
Added dated UN 2024 figures instead of undated generic statements.

sourceRecords.title: Demographic Transition: Why is rapid population growth a temporary phenomenon?
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the five-stage structure, the asynchronous timing of mortality and fertility decline that opens the 'growth gap', Stage 3 drivers (improved child survival, economic change, female autonomy), and the explicit uncertainty about Stage 5 (few societies have reached very high development). Historical anchors: England and Wales gap opening after 1750 with Stage 3 around the 1870s; Sweden's death rate declining from ~1800 with birth rates constant until the 1860s. Facts synthesized in original prose; no charts or passages reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 4.4: The Demographic Transition Model (Human Demography)
sourceRecords.provider: LibreTexts / GALILEO Open Learning Materials (Zehnder, Manoylov, Mutiti, Mutiti, VandeVoort, Bennett)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports the four-stage description and drivers: Stage 1 high/high; Stage 2 death rates fall from medical advances, sanitation, and food production while births stay high; Stage 3 births fall as women enter the workforce, children become economically costly, and birth control access rises; Stage 4 low/low at ~2 children per couple. Explicitly states the model was built on patterns observed in European countries and that not all countries fit it exactly. Non-commercial share-alike license, so treated as reference-only: facts synthesized, no wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: UN projects world population to peak within this century (World Population Prospects 2024)
sourceRecords.provider: United Nations (Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division)
sourceRecords.notes: Supports dated 2024 figures: world population about 8.2 billion in 2024; projected peak around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, declining to roughly 10.2 billion by 2100; replacement level about 2.1 births per woman; more than half of all countries and areas already below replacement, with 'ultra-low' fertility (under 1.4) in nearly one-fifth of countries. Also notes replacement is the level that maintains population size 'without migration', supporting the point that the classic model brackets migration. Reference-only; facts restated in original prose.
